title: Voice Leading
intro: Voice leading is the art of moving each note of one chord to a note of the next so that every part makes a good melody of its own and the parts stay independent. The rules come from four-part vocal writing (soprano, alto, tenor, bass), but they underlie good piano and band arranging too.

blocks.text: Chorales and harmony exercises use four voices with these ranges: soprano C4–G5, alto G3–D5, tenor C3–G4, bass E2–C4. Adjacent upper voices stay within an octave of each other (tenor and bass can be further apart). With four voices and three notes in a triad, one note is doubled; in root position the root is the normal choice, and the leading tone is never doubled (it has to resolve up to the tonic, and doubling it forces parallel octaves or a wrong resolution).

items: Keep common tones: a note shared by both chords stays in the same voice.
Move the other voices by the smallest possible interval, mostly by step.
Resolve tendency tones: the leading tone rises to the tonic (in an inner voice it may fall to 5̂); the seventh of a chord falls by step.
Prefer contrary motion between the soprano and bass, especially at cadences.
Avoid voice crossing and overlapping: each voice stays above the one below it and does not move past where the neighbouring voice just was.

blocks.text: Two voices a perfect fifth or octave apart that move in the same direction to another perfect fifth or octave are parallel fifths or octaves. They were avoided because they make the two voices fuse into one, losing their independence: an octave pair is heard as one thicker line, and parallel fifths sound hollow and archaic (they are the sound of medieval organum, and of rock power chords). Hidden (direct) fifths and octaves, where the outer voices reach a perfect interval in similar motion with a leap in the soprano, are avoided between the outer voices too.

widget.title: Parallel fifths versus good voice leading for IV–V

examples.label: Parallel fifths and octaves (all voices move up)
Correct: upper voices move down against the bass

blocks.text: The standard solution for IV–V and V–vi (roots a step apart) is to move the three upper voices in contrary motion to the bass, to the nearest chord tones.

In four parts a seventh chord can use all four notes, or omit the fifth and double the root. The seventh resolves down by step: in V7–I, the 7th (4̂) falls to 3̂ and the leading tone (7̂) rises to 1̂. A complete V7 resolving to a complete I would need one of those to break its tendency, so usually one of the two chords is incomplete (no fifth).

Keyboard style puts the bass alone in the left hand and the three upper voices in the right hand, within an octave. It is the practical way to play hymns and chorales and to accompany singers. The same principles apply: common tones held, nearest-note motion, tendency tones resolved.

blocks.title: Find the error
blocks.text: In C major, a progression moves from F–A–C–F (bass to soprano: F3, C4, F4, A4) to G–B–D–G (G3, D4, G4, B4). What is wrong?
solution: Bass F3→G3, tenor C4→D4, alto F4→G4, soprano A4→B4: every voice moves up a step. Bass and alto make parallel octaves (F–F to G–G), bass and tenor parallel fifths (F–C to G–D).

blocks.title: Resolve V7
blocks.text: In D major, resolve this V7 to I. Voices, bass to soprano: A2, G3, E4, C♯5.
solution: A7 is A C♯ E G and the chord is complete. The bass A2 goes to D3. The 7th, G3, falls by step to F♯3. The leading tone C♯5 rises to D5. E4, the fifth, falls to D4 by step.
Result: D3, F♯3, D4, D5. The tonic is incomplete (three roots, a third, no fifth), the normal outcome when a complete V7 resolves with every tendency tone obeyed.

McGraw-Hill; Laitz, S. G. (2016). The Complete Musician, 4th ed. Oxford University Press; Huron, D. (2001). Tone and voice: a derivation of the rules of voice-leading from perceptual principles.
